definition: Bad data silently corrupts every decision downstream — the cost compounds far past the pipeline.
explanation: A wrong join or null spike doesn't error; it ships. Dashboards mislead, ML models train on garbage, and trust erodes. Catching issues at the source is orders of magnitude cheaper than debugging a bad decision later.
interviewLine: Data quality matters because bad data fails silently and propagates — the cost of catching it early is far below the cost of a wrong decision.
whyItMatters: 'Garbage in, garbage out' is why data-quality engineering is now a first-class discipline.

definition: The measurable facets of quality: completeness, accuracy, consistency, timeliness, validity, uniqueness.
explanation: Completeness: no missing values. Accuracy: matches reality. Consistency: agrees across systems. Timeliness: fresh enough. Validity: conforms to rules/types. Uniqueness: no unwanted duplicates. Each maps to a concrete check.
interviewLine: Quality has dimensions — completeness, accuracy, consistency, timeliness, validity, uniqueness — each becoming a concrete automated check.
whyItMatters: Naming dimensions turns vague 'data is bad' into specific, testable assertions.
interviewQuestion: Which dimension does a freshness SLA measure?

definition: Explicit checks that gate data: assert conditions and fail (or quarantine) the run when they break.
explanation: Validation encodes expectations as assertions — row counts in range, no nulls in a key, referential integrity — and runs them in the pipeline. A failed assertion blocks promotion so bad data never reaches consumers.
interviewLine: Validation asserts expectations (ranges, non-null keys, referential integrity) in-pipeline and blocks promotion when they fail.
whyItMatters: Assertions turn quality from a hope into a build gate that stops bad data at the door.

definition: A Python framework for declaring, running, and documenting 'expectations' about data.
explanation: You build an expectation suite (e.g. expect_column_values_to_not_be_null) and run it against a batch; GE validates, produces data-docs, and can fail the pipeline. It centralizes checks and their results as living documentation.
interviewLine: Great Expectations declares reusable 'expectations' about data, validates batches against them, and generates docs plus pass/fail gates.
whyItMatters: It's the best-known dedicated data-validation tool — a common interview name-drop.

definition: Data-quality checks that run inside the warehouse as part of the dbt build.
explanation: dbt's generic tests (unique, not_null, accepted_values, relationships) and singular SQL tests assert quality on transformed models and gate CI. Quality lives next to the transformation code, versioned together.
interviewLine: dbt tests assert quality in-warehouse (unique, not_null, relationships, custom SQL) as a build gate, co-located with the models.
whyItMatters: For ELT stacks, dbt tests are the lowest-friction place to enforce quality — no extra tool.

definition: The two most common quality checks: no unexpected nulls in key columns, and no duplicate keys.
explanation: A null in a join key drops rows; a duplicate primary key double-counts. These basic assertions (not_null, unique) catch the majority of real-world breakages and are the first tests to add to any model.
interviewLine: Null and duplicate checks guard keys — nulls silently drop join rows and dup keys double-count, so not_null/unique are the first tests to add.
whyItMatters: Most production data incidents trace back to an unexpected null or a broken uniqueness assumption.
commonMistake: Testing uniqueness on a column that legitimately repeats, or missing that a composite key is what's actually unique.

definition: Verifying data arrived recently enough — alerting when the newest record is older than an SLA.
explanation: A pipeline can run 'successfully' yet load nothing if the source stalled. Freshness checks compare max(loaded_at) or max(event_time) against a threshold and alert on staleness, catching silent upstream failures.
interviewLine: Freshness checks alert when the newest data exceeds an age SLA, catching silent stalls where the job 'succeeds' but loads nothing new.
whyItMatters: Stale-but-present data is the sneakiest failure — no error, just wrong-because-old dashboards.
interviewQuestion: Why can a green pipeline run still have stale data?

definition: Enforcing that incoming data matches an expected structure — columns, types, and constraints.
explanation: Before loading, validate the payload against a schema (types, required fields, enums). Reject or quarantine records that don't conform, often backed by a schema registry so producers and consumers agree on structure.
interviewLine: Schema validation enforces expected columns, types, and constraints at the boundary, rejecting or quarantining nonconforming records.
whyItMatters: Structural guarantees stop malformed data from silently poisoning downstream transforms.

definition: A formal, versioned agreement between a data producer and its consumers on schema, semantics, and SLAs.
explanation: A contract pins what a producer guarantees — fields, types, meaning, freshness, and how changes are versioned — enforced in CI so a breaking change is caught before it ships. It shifts quality left, to the source.
interviewLine: A data contract is a versioned producer-consumer agreement on schema, semantics, and SLAs, enforced in CI so breaking changes fail before shipping.
whyItMatters: Contracts are the hot fix for the root cause of most quality issues: unannounced producer changes.
interviewQuestion: How does a data contract shift quality enforcement 'left'?

definition: Monitoring pipeline health across five pillars: freshness, volume, schema, distribution, and lineage.
explanation: Borrowed from software observability: track whether data is on time (freshness), the right amount (volume), the right shape (schema), within normal ranges (distribution), and how it flows (lineage) — to detect incidents automatically.
interviewLine: Data observability monitors five pillars — freshness, volume, schema, distribution, lineage — to auto-detect incidents beyond explicit tests.
whyItMatters: Observability tools (Monte Carlo, etc.) catch unknown-unknowns that hand-written tests miss.

definition: Statistically learning a metric's normal range and alerting when new data drifts outside it.
explanation: Instead of fixed thresholds, fit the historical pattern (mean/stddev, seasonality) of row counts, null rates, or value distributions and flag deviations. Catches issues you didn't know to write a rule for.
interviewLine: Anomaly detection models a metric's normal range (with seasonality) and alerts on drift, catching issues no fixed rule anticipated.
whyItMatters: It scales quality to metrics no one thought to assert on — the unknown-unknowns.
commonMistake: Alerting on raw thresholds that ignore seasonality — Monday traffic looks like an 'anomaly' every week.

definition: Comparing source and target to prove no rows or values were lost or altered in transit.
explanation: After a load, reconcile: row counts, key sets, and control totals (sums of amounts) between source and target must match. Mismatches reveal dropped rows, dupes, or transform bugs before anyone trusts the numbers.
interviewLine: Reconciliation compares source vs target on counts, keys, and control totals to prove the load lost or changed nothing.
whyItMatters: Reconciliation is the audit that turns 'the job ran' into 'the data is provably complete'.

definition: Isolating failing records into a separate area so good data flows while bad data is held for review.
explanation: Rather than failing the whole batch, route invalid rows to a quarantine table/topic with the reason. Clean data proceeds; quarantined rows are inspected, fixed, and replayed — balancing throughput against strictness.
interviewLine: Quarantine isolates invalid rows (with a failure reason) so clean data flows while bad records wait to be fixed and replayed.
whyItMatters: Quarantine avoids the false choice between blocking the pipeline and shipping bad rows.

definition: Scanning a dataset to summarize its shape — value ranges, null rates, cardinality, distributions.
explanation: Before writing checks you must know the data: profiling computes per-column stats (min/max, distinct count, null %, top values) so you can set realistic expectations and spot obvious problems immediately.
interviewLine: Profiling summarizes a dataset's columns — ranges, null rates, cardinality, distributions — to ground realistic quality expectations.
whyItMatters: Profiling is the first step of any quality effort — you can't assert on data you don't understand.
